**Fuel Cell**

![](/content/exams/anzca/2015/B/13/standard-image17.png){fig-alt="Fuel cell oxygen analyser with lead anode, gold cathode and potassium hydroxide solution"}

Fuel cells rely on reduction of oxygen to measure oxygen partial pressure. They consist of:

- Oxygen permeable membrane
- KOH solution, within in which is a:
  - Lead anode - Lead is consumed as the fuel cell operates
  - Gold cathode

Method

- Oxygen diffuses across the membrane into the potassium hydroxide solution
- At the cathode: O~2~ + 4e^-^ + 2H~2~O → 4OH^-^
- At the anode: 2Pb + 4OH^-^ → 4PbO + 2H~2~O + 4^e-^
- The oxygen consumption is proportional to the current generated, which is measured with an ammeter

#### Pros

- No power required
- Cheap
- Accurate
- Used for gas or blood 

#### Cons

- Lifespan 6-12 months
- Requires regular two-point calibration with 21% and 100% oxygen.
- Relatively slow response time compared to paramagnetic analysers \~20s.

 **Paramagnetic Analyser**

![](/content/exams/anzca/2015/B/13/standard-image18.png){fig-alt="Paramagnetic oxygen analyser using alternating magnetic field and differential pressure measurement"}

Principles of paramagnetic analysis:

- Oxygen is paramagnetic\
  This means it is attracted by magnetic fields, but does not propagate the field. 
  - This is because it has two unpaired outer shell electrons being spun in same direction
  - Many other gases weakly repelled by magnetic fields (diamagnetic)
- The attraction of a gas mixture to a magnetic field is therefore proportional to its oxygen content
- Different methods exist which use this property to determine oxygen content

#### Pros

- Accurate
- Rapid response time - Modern analysers can identify breath-to-breath variation in FiO2.
- Don't require regular calibration

#### Cons

- For Gas only 
- Water vapour reduces accuracy
- Interference from other paramagnetic gases
  - Nitric oxide\
    Effect is minimal as nitric is delivered in far smaller volumes than oxygen, and is only weakly paramagnetic.
